# Rear Right Drum Brake Overheating: Diagnosing and Fixing Asymmetric Heat Distribution

A single brake drum running significantly hotter than its counterpart is rarely "normal," regardless of what a mechanic might casually suggest. In the specific case of a Tata Tiago exhibiting excessive heat on the rear right side while the left side remains cool, this indicates an imbalance in energy dissipation or hydraulic pressure distribution. While the absence of noise after cleaning shoes and replacing ABS components was encouraging, the persistent thermal asymmetry points to underlying mechanical or hydraulic faults that require deeper investigation.

When a drum brake system generates heat unevenly, it usually stems from one of three core issues: dragging brakes, improper shoe alignment, or a failing wheel cylinder. The fact that the sound has disappeared after replacing the ABS module suggests the electronic actuation is no longer locking the caliper or causing intermittent drag. However, thermal energy generation in drum brakes follows simple physics: kinetic energy must convert to heat. If one side consistently converts more energy into heat than the other, the friction coefficient or the duration of contact between the shoe and the drum differs significantly.

One common culprit is the wheel cylinder itself. Drum brakes utilize hydraulic pressure to push shoes outward against the drum. If the right-side wheel cylinder has a sticking piston or internal seal degradation, it may not retract fully after braking. Even a millimeter of drag generates enough friction to cause noticeable heating over a short drive. This condition often lacks audible symptoms until the heat becomes palpable, precisely matching your observation that the noise is gone but the heat remains. The previous mechanic likely cleaned the shoes and replaced the ABS unit, addressing the symptom (noise) and assuming the cause (drag), but did not isolate the hydraulic component responsible for the persistent drag on that specific side.

Another possibility involves the shoe-to-spring ratio or self-adjuster mechanism failure. Drum brakes are designed to auto-adjust as the lining wears. If the self-adjuster on the right side is malfunctioning, it might be pushing the shoes too close to the drum at rest, creating constant friction. This scenario can also occur if the return springs are weak or broken, failing to pull the shoes back when the pedal is released.

To diagnose this without relying solely on visual inspection, you can perform a manual retraction test. With the wheels lifted and safely supported, remove the rear right wheel and inspect the drum's interior. Manually push the pistons of the wheel cylinder inward using a C-clamp or brake caliper spreader (with caution). If the pistons feel stiff or do not move smoothly with consistent pressure, the seals are likely compromised. Rebuilding the wheel cylinder is often more cost-effective than replacing it entirely, as internal corrosion can be cleaned out before resealing.

Additionally, verify that the parking brake cable tension is balanced. Excessive tension on one side can mechanically force the shoes outward. While less common in modern cars like the Tiago compared to older models with mechanical handbrakes integrated into the drum assembly, it remains a potential source of asymmetry if the linkage binding occurs only under specific suspension angles.

The decision to replace the ABS module was valid given the noise, but it does not explain the thermal imbalance. The real fix lies in isolating the right-side rear brake assembly for a full rebuild: replacing wheel cylinder seals, inspecting return springs for elasticity, and ensuring the self-adjuster is functioning correctly. Ignoring this heat buildup risks glazing the brake lining, reducing stopping power, and eventually warping the drum itself. Addressing these mechanical nuances ensures the vehicle maintains consistent braking performance without hidden thermal risks.
